sections.h2: Who do you contact about a Lee County tax bill?
sections.html:
Four desks inside one courthouse in Dixon split the job. Questions about value or exemptions belong with the assessment staff, payment trouble goes to the Treasurer, and a question about how a rate came out goes to the Clerk's extension department.

Lee County offices that touch a property tax bill, per leecountyil.com
OfficeRoleContact
Treasurer and CollectorPrints and collects bills, runs the annual tax sale, administers senior deferral815-288-4477, 112 E Second Street, mailing box 328
Chief County Assessment OfficeValues, exemptions, appeal paperwork815-288-4483, open weekdays from 8 until 4:30
Board of ReviewDecides assessment complaints815-288-4483, first floor of the old courthouse
County Clerk and RecorderExtends rates, takes redemption money after a sale, records deeds815-288-3309, mailing box 329

The Treasurer reports collecting and passing along more than $96 million this year to over 130 taxing districts. That explains why a Lee County bill reads like a ledger of school, township, fire and county lines rather than one charge.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Lee County itself?
sections.html:
Lee County lies along the Rock River country of northern Illinois and was carved out of Ogle County on February 27, 1839. Dixon, where Ronald Reagan spent part of his boyhood, is the seat and the biggest city. Amboy is the other incorporated city the county lists, while Rochelle lies mostly across the line in Ogle County. Land area is roughly 725 square miles, and the neighbors are Ogle, DeKalb, LaSalle, Bureau and Whiteside.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 32,914 people, a drop from the 34,145 counted in 2020. Of occupied homes, 73.6% have owners living in them. The midpoint value for an owner-occupied home in the 2020 to 2024 survey is $154,600, and the midpoint household income is $70,292. Builders took out just 32 permits in 2025. An EF4 tornado touched down here on April 9, 2015, so storm history is a fair question for a buyer.

Several school districts cut across the county, including Dixon Unit 170, Amboy 272, Ashton 275, Lee Center 271, Polo 222 and Sterling 5. Whichever one serves your address drives much of the rate.

sections.h2: How are Lee County homes valued for tax?
sections.html:
Township assessors propose values, and the county assessment office pulls them together. The target for houses is one-third of fair cash value. When a single parcel changes, the office mails a notice. When the only change comes from a township-wide equalization factor, no notice is required.

Illinois runs on a four-year general reassessment. The county's publication page names Amboy, Ashton, Bradford, Franklin Grove, Nachusa, Lee Center, May and Sublette as the townships in their general year for 2026. Anyone can look over a parcel's size, age, lot and sketch at the assessment counter, or search property record cards on the county site.

A bigger bill does not always mean a bigger assessment. The county's FAQ gives three general explanations: a taxing district asked for more, an exemption you qualify for has not been applied, or other owners picked up exemptions you lack. The county itself can only set its own levy. Under the state's extension limitation law, most districts may grow their levy by the smaller of 5% or inflation over the highest of the prior three years, and new construction, bonds and referendum-approved increases sit outside that cap.

sections.h2: What is the process to contest a Lee County value?
sections.html:
You file a written complaint with the Board of Review within 30 calendar days of the assessment list being published, as 35 ILCS 200/16-55 requires. For the townships named above, the county lists November 18, 2026 as the publication date and December 18, 2026 as the last day to file. Townships not on that list have their own publication dates, so ask the assessment staff which applies to you.

Three members, chosen by the County Board, sit on the Board of Review, and they may confirm, lower or raise a value. The county's FAQ says its rules accept these grounds:

  • Equity, meaning your value out of line with similar homes
  • Fair cash value
  • A wrong physical description of the property
  • Questions of law

Speak with your township assessor or the county staff beforehand, since many disputes end in that conversation. After the 30 days, only a physical-data mismatch, such as a house recorded larger than it is, can still be raised. If the Board's ruling disappoints you, the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board takes the next step at 217-782-6076 or 401 S Spring Street, Room 402, Springfield. The Board looks at value only, so an objection to the size of the final bill belongs with the taxing districts.

sections.h2: How do you pay Lee County real estate tax?
sections.html:
The state splits the bill in two, and the county prints each due date on the bill itself. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-15, a first installment turns delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day following the printed date. The second follows the same test against September 1. Late interest is 1 1/2% for each month or fraction. A mailed payment with a postmark on or before the date counts as on time.

Ways to pay include:

  • The county's property tax inquiry website, which shows a pay link after you search by PIN, owner name or address.
  • Phone payment at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 7042.
  • A check mailed to Lee County Collector, P.O. Box 328, Dixon, IL 61021.
  • The Treasurer's counter at the Old Lee County Courthouse.

The county's due-dates page states a 2.40% card fee through a third party with a $2.00 floor. For e-checks it prints $2 up to $50,000, then $4, $8.50 and $10 in higher bands. If you never received a bill, ask the Treasurer for a duplicate, since a missing bill does not cancel the debt. Send address updates on the county's change-of-address form.

sections.h2: Which Lee County breaks reduce a bill?
sections.html:
An exemption subtracts from equalized assessed value ahead of the rate. Because Lee County does not border a county with 3,000,000 or more residents, the lower statutory ceilings apply. These are the main ones:

  • General homestead: a reduction of as much as $6,000 on a home the owner lives in (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • Senior citizens: as much as $5,000 once the owner turns 65 within the assessment year (35 ILCS 200/15-170). The county's form says the exemption renews on its own after approval, and owners must tell the office if the home stops qualifying.
  • Senior freeze: a yearly application, with household income held under the limit on the county form.
  • Tax deferral: the Treasurer's program for owners 65 and over whose household income is at most $75,000, moving to $77,000 for tax year 2026 and $79,000 for 2027. The postponed tax rides as a lien until the house sells.

File exemption forms with the assessment office. After a sale, state law keeps the seller's homestead credit through the assessment year of the sale, and the office can ask the buyer to apply for the year after.

sections.h2: What if the Lee County bill goes unpaid?
sections.html:
What gets sold is the unpaid tax, not your home. Each year the Treasurer puts every unpaid parcel into a tax sale. You keep the right to redeem by paying the tax with added costs and interest, and the redemption desk sits in the County Clerk's office.

State law usually gives three years from the sale date, subject to exceptions in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. If a buyer already holds a certificate on your parcel, get the Clerk's payoff figure and final date in writing before you set a price or sign a contract.

sections.h2: How do taxes settle at a Lee County closing?
sections.html:
A title agent or attorney reads the latest bill, checks for installments still open, and divides the year between seller and buyer on the closing statement. Before that, ask the Treasurer whether any older year is delinquent or sold, since that balance must be cleared at the table. When a lender escrows taxes, find out which installments it has remitted.

Houses that come with probate, tenants or deferred repairs often carry back taxes too. A payoff letter from the Treasurer, together with a redemption figure from the Clerk if a sale happened, lets you weigh competing offers on equal terms.

faqs.q: Which number reaches the Lee County Treasurer?
faqs.a: 815-288-4477 for bills and payments. The assessment office at 815-288-4483 takes value, exemption and appeal questions, and the Clerk's extension department at 815-288-3309 explains how rates are built and handles redemption.

faqs.q: Is there any way to appeal late in Lee County?
faqs.a: Only for a physical-data error. The county's FAQ says complaints must come within 30 days of the roll's publication, with the single exception of a mismatch like the wrong square footage on the record.

faqs.q: What is the largest general homestead reduction in Lee County?
faqs.a: $6,000 of equalized assessed value, since the county does not border one with 3,000,000 or more inhabitants. The rule is 35 ILCS 200/15-175, and the assessment office takes the application.

faqs.q: What does late payment cost in Lee County?
faqs.a: Interest of 1 1/2% per month or partial month under 35 ILCS 200/21-15. The clock starts after the later of the statutory date or the day after the printed due date, and a timely postmark avoids it.

faqs.q: Does Lee County's senior deferral wipe out the tax?
faqs.a: No, it only delays it. The deferred amount becomes a lien and comes due when the house is sold. An applicant must be 65 or older and apply through the Treasurer, whose page states the income limit.
